Sit down, Chinmay, let me tell you about Sir Vishwas. I'm Vidya. When I was fifteen and already taller than my mother, my science teacher would say, "Careful, sweetheart, don't touch, this is not a toy," and hand me the microscope slide like I was five. It made me furious. I stopped answering, I rolled my eyes and once I wrote a rude word in my notebook.
Then Sir Vishwas took over. First day he said, "Vidya, you've read ahead. What do you think is wrong with this experiment?" I nearly fell off my stool. I worked like a horse for him.

qa.q: What did the first science teacher say when handing Vidya the microscope slide?
qa.a: The teacher said, "Careful, sweetheart, don't touch, this is not a toy."

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when the science teacher spoke to Vidya like a five-year-old?
qa.a: Vidya felt disrespected and furious. Stopping answering, rolling eyes and writing a rude word show how the anger turned into defiance.

qa.q: What changed when Sir Vishwas took over, and why did it matter to Vidya?
qa.a: Sir Vishwas asked Vidya's own opinion about what was wrong with the experiment. Being treated as someone with real ideas made Vidya want to work hard.

qa.q: How might the first science teacher have seen Vidya's rude behaviour?
qa.a: The first teacher may have thought Vidya was just being rude, without seeing that "sweetheart" felt babyish. Treating Vidya as a young adult might have avoided the anger.

grounding: A teenager addressed like a small child feels disrespected and turns defiant, until a teacher asks for opinions, told by the elder as a memory.

Twenty minutes before the science fair judges arrived, the hall was loud with drills and trolley wheels. Salma stood over her circuit board, tongue between her teeth.
Mahima, the physics teacher, bustled over. "Ooh, let Ma'am do the wiring, sweetheart. You just hold the battery, okay?"
Salma folded her arms. "I built this, Ma'am. Give it back."
"Don't be rude."
Salma turned to leave. Mahima took a breath. "Wait. I'm sorry. Talk me through your reasoning. The layout is your call, you decide."
Salma looked at her, then pointed to a wire. "That one is loose, it needs to go here."
They fixed it with ten minutes to spare.

qa.q: How many minutes before the judges arrived did the scene begin?
qa.a: The scene began twenty minutes before the science fair judges arrived.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling when Mahima said "let Ma'am do the wiring, sweetheart"?
qa.a: Salma felt disrespected and defiant. Folding arms and saying "I built this" show anger at being treated like a small child.

qa.q: What did Mahima change after Salma turned to leave, and what was the result?
qa.a: Mahima apologised and asked Salma to explain the reasoning, saying the layout was Salma's call. Salma then pointed out the loose wire, and they fixed it in time.

qa.q: How might Mahima have seen the moment Salma said "Give it back"?
qa.a: Mahima probably felt flustered under the time pressure and saw it as rudeness at first. Taking a breath let Mahima realise Salma wanted to be heard.

grounding: A teenager addressed like a small child by a teacher feels disrespected and turns defiant, until the teacher treats them as a capable young adult.

passage:
I'm Saurabh, and in Class 10 we had a new physics teacher, Harish Sir, who talked to us like we were in nursery. "Now, children, who can tell me what a magnet does? Very good, beta, clap for him." In front of everyone.
When I asked a real question about why the Earth has a magnetic field, he said, "Such big questions from a small boy! Let's stick to the chapter."
Something in me went hard. After that I sat at the back and made comments. I stopped doing homework. I knew it was childish, but it felt like the only way to be taken seriously.
In Class 11, Mrs Kaur taught us. On day one she said, "You're almost adults. I'll expect a lot and I'll listen." When I asked about the Earth's field, she said, "Great question. Find three sources and teach it to us Friday."
I did. It was the best week of that year.

qa.q: What did Harish Sir say when Saurabh asked about the Earth's magnetic field?
qa.a: He said, "Such big questions from a small boy! Let's stick to the chapter."

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling after Harish Sir called it a big question from a small boy?
qa.a: Saurabh felt humiliated and disrespected, and that hurt hardened into defiance.

qa.q: What did Mrs Kaur do differently, and why did it draw cooperation?
qa.a: She treated the class as almost adults, took Saurabh's question seriously and gave him real responsibility, so he had no need to rebel.

qa.q: What would change if Harish Sir had welcomed Saurabh's question?
qa.a: Saurabh would likely have felt respected and stayed engaged in physics instead of turning to comments at the back.

grounding: A teenager addressed like a small child by a teacher turns defiant, and a teacher who treats him as a developing adult draws cooperation.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Thursday
Francis, Class 9, was sent to me for the third time this month for "attitude". I asked him what happened. He said the vice principal had stopped him in the corridor about his untucked shirt and said, loudly, "Who's a naughty boy today? Should I call Mummy?" His friends laughed. Francis answered, "Call whoever you like," and walked off.
He told me, "I'm fifteen. I'd have tucked it in if she'd just told me."
I spoke to Ms Disha, his new class teacher, who has had no trouble with him. She said she asks his opinion on class decisions and he usually helps.
What I did next: I shared this with the vice principal, suggested speaking to Class 9 students plainly and privately, and set up a short meeting where Francis can explain himself calmly. He agreed to come.

qa.q: What did the vice principal say to Francis in the corridor?
qa.a: She said, loudly, "Who's a naughty boy today? Should I call Mummy?"

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he answered back?
qa.a: Francis felt humiliated and disrespected in front of his friends, which turned into angry defiance.

qa.q: What would you advise adults dealing with Francis?
qa.a: Speak to him plainly and privately, as Ms Disha does, ask his opinion and treat him as a developing adult, which draws his help.

qa.q: How does Ms Disha see Francis?
qa.a: Ms Disha sees him as helpful and capable, because she treats his opinions as real.

grounding: An adult's note shows a teenager talked down to like a small child turning defiant, while respect draws cooperation.

passage:
Saturday night
Rehana Phuppo came for Nikhat's engagement and pinched my cheek in front of EVERYONE. "Look at our little Sahil! Do you still like chocolate, baby?" I'm sixteen. I'm taller than her.
Then at dinner, when the uncles were talking about the election, I said something, and she said, "Arre, children don't understand these things. Go eat your ice cream."
I got up and said, "Maybe I understand more than you think," and left the table. Ammi gave me the look.
Later Phuppo came to the terrace. She actually said sorry. She said, "You've grown up and I didn't notice." Then she asked me what I really thought about the election. We talked for twenty minutes. She even said, "That's a good point."
I told her I'd help her with the decorations tomorrow. Weird how it flipped.

qa.q: How old is Sahil?
qa.a: Sahil says, "I'm sixteen."

qa.q: Why did Sahil leave the dinner table?
qa.a: Sahil felt disrespected and angry at being called a child who couldn't understand, so Sahil answered back and walked away.

qa.q: What did Phuppo do on the terrace that changed things?
qa.a: Phuppo apologised, admitted not noticing that Sahil had grown up, and asked Sahil's real opinion, treating Sahil as a developing adult.

qa.q: How did Rehana Phuppo likely feel on the terrace?
qa.a: Rehana Phuppo likely felt sorry and a little surprised, realising Sahil had grown up without her noticing.

grounding: A teenager talked down to by a relative turns defiant, and being asked for a real opinion draws cooperation.
